transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-15 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~46 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Romano (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Dave Nguyen (Orion CTO), Sara Morales (Orion Sr Cloud Eng), Evan Price (Orion Security), Liam O'Connor (PM)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Dave: yep good here, thanks for setting this up.
[00:06] Maya: cool, quick round intros then we'll jump in - im an AE at Redwood, Luca and Priya are our solutions folks, and you can run through roles on your side?
[00:12] Dave: im dave cto, sara is our cloud engineer, evan handles security, liam product.
[00:18] Maya: perfect. objective today is to understand your VPC/network constraints and whether Private deployment makes sense vs Dedicated/Hosted. also align on next steps for a pilot.
[00:27] Sara: great. background: we're evaluating LLM infra for customer-facing features. data residency and no internet egress are hard requirements for regulated customers in eu-west and us-east. we want private connectivity to the model endpoints; public internet is not allowed.
[00:41] Luca: got it. can you confirm whether you want Redwood managed control plane in our cloud with PrivateLink, or a fully customer-managed on-prem stack?
[00:48] Evan: preference is private control plane in our accounts - so vendor provides the runtime but we keep the VPCs and keys. basically Private deployment with customer-controlled networking and KMS.
[00:59] Priya: ok that's the common pattern. quick note - Redwood Private can be deployed with a customer VPC and private endpoints; we support both VPC peering and PrivateLink (interface endpoints) depending on topology and security posture.
[01:12] Liam: can you explain the tradeoffs? we've seen both used but not sure which suits multi-account orgs.
[01:18] Luca: sure. VPC peering is simple point-to-point, low latency, but it doesn't scale well for many accounts and cross-region peering has limits and extra routing complexity. PrivateLink/Private endpoints allow central service exposure into customer VPCs via ENIs and are nice for multi-account because you don't need transitive routing; they also integrate with endpoint policies. for large fleets we often recommend Transit Gateway + peering or PrivateLink depending on route controls.
[01:40] Sara: transit gateway is our org standard; we use TGW for cross-account attachments. we also have strict egress rules - only specific NATs allowed, and S3 endpoints are used for storage. how does Redwood handle outbound calls from the runtime?
[01:52] Priya: runtime egress can be tightly controlled. for Private deployments we support egress through customer NAT or VPC endpoints only. we can disable internet access and allow connections to customer-managed services only. for S3 we support VPC gateway endpoints and we can place the runtime in private subnets.
[02:06] Evan: KMS - we require customer-managed CMKs in our AWS account (HSM-backed) for any persisted artifacts and logs. will Redwood bring keys into your KMS or can we keep keys?
[02:16] Luca: we integrate with customer KMS. Redwood's control plane can be deployed as a thin control plane if you prefer, but for private deployments we support using customer CMKs; logs and data at rest can be encrypted with your keys. some customers elect to have Redwood manage ephemeral keys for runtime, but for compliance we can wire up your KMS/HSM.
[02:31] Dave: region constraints - we need services in eu-west-1 and us-east-1 only. cannot have data stored outside. are there any limitations to running Redwood in those regions?
[02:41] Priya: we support eu-west-1 and us-east-1. difference is hardware availability; certain GPU instance types might vary. if you need very low latency we can provision Dedicated nodes in both regions. in Private deployment we can place the runtime in your VPC in those regions.
[02:55] Liam: latency expectations - target p95 inference latency of <250ms for chat traffic (mostly short prompts). is that achievable with Private in-region setup?
[03:02] Luca: yes for small- to mid-size models; for larger models p95 can be higher. Dedicated capacity with batching configs and KV cache helps. key is keeping model and serving capacity in same AZs near your frontends. we can run a pilot with representative qps to validate.
[03:18] Sara: about networking details - do you require public IPs on the runtime instances? we try to avoid public addresses.
[03:24] Priya: no public IPs required. runtime lives in private subnets, we use ENIs for PrivateLink or peering. NAT only if you need egress to external services; otherwise zero internet.
[03:34] Evan: audit logs - we need audit trails, immutable logs with retention policies and integration with our SIEM. is that supported?
[03:40] Luca: yes. Redwood can push audit logs to your S3 or CloudWatch; we support signed audit logs, and you can retain them per your policy. we can also stream to your Kinesis or EventBridge. logs can be encrypted with your CMKs.
[03:53] Dave: how does authentication work? SSO, RBAC?
[03:56] Maya: we support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, role-based access. for Private deployments you can integrate with your IdP and use your IAM roles for service accounts.
[04:04] Sara: has there been production customers using TGW + PrivateLink with Redwood? any gotchas?
[04:09] Priya: yes, several. gotcha is route table limits and propagation. when using Transit Gateway you need to ensure route table scale and ENI limits are addressed; also security groups need to be opened between ENIs and runtime subnets. we provide a network runbook and a checklist.
[04:23] Evan: are there IP allowlists on Redwood side or do we do mutual TLS?
[04:28] Luca: both. you can do security at network layer (peer/PrivateLink + SGs) and at transport layer with mTLS for service-to-service. for some customers we also do client certs for API calls; others rely on private endpoints and IAM.
[04:39] Liam: curious about failover - if region goes down, is automatic fallback to hosted possible or do we need manual steps?
[04:46] Priya: we recommend explicit routing/failover policies. Redwood's smart routing can failover to another region or model variant, but for Private you control routing. some customers implement a cross-region transit and a warm standby. we can help design a canary/fallback plan.
[04:58] Dave: cost question - how does Private compare to Dedicated?
[05:02] Maya: Dedicated is reserved capacity in Redwood-managed infra; Private runs in your VPC and often has higher initial infra ops but gives you control and compliance. TCO depends on committed usage, instance selection, and whether you need multi-region replication. we'll send a TCO comparison.
[05:16] Sara: network performance - we need 10k requests per minute in peak, with median tokens per request low. will the Private deployment handle autoscaling?
[05:26] Luca: yes, autoscaling supported; metrics-driven. for high QPS we suggest a mix of small GRU-style batching nodes and a KV cache layer to reduce per-token compute. scheduler supports horizontal scaling; we'll define autoscale thresholds in the pilot.
[05:39] Evan: security review - we will run our standard vendor security checklist. do you have SOC2/ISO docs and pen test reports?
[05:46] Maya: yes, we'll share SOC2 and ISO attestation, pen test summary, and a network runbook. we can sign an NDA if needed.
[05:54] Dave: operational concerns - who is on-call for the runtime? how are incidents handled?
[05:58] Priya: for Redwood Private, support tiers vary. typically Redwood ops is on-call for platform issues if we host control plane components; for runtime in customer VPC you can opt for managed support where Redwood handles incident response with access. SLA options available.
[06:12] Liam: do you need console access into our VPC for debugging?
[06:16] Luca: not normally; we use logs, metrics, and remote playbooks. if deeper debugging needed we can request temporary access via your jump host or SSM with audit. many customers prefer to do packet captures themselves and share sanitized outputs.
[06:28] Sara: what's the smallest pilot we can run to validate network and latency?
[06:32] Maya: typical pilot: 1) deploy runtime in a single account + region in a subset of subnets, 2) sample traffic (10-50 qps) with representative prompts, 3) telemetry collection for 2 weeks. Luca will define exact qps and token distributions.
[06:45] Luca: for the bench plan i'll ask for sample payloads, QPS, average tokens, and topologies (TGW vs peering). will also include steps for enabling ENIs and SG rules.
[06:55] Evan: how are secrets handled for model weights and configs?
[06:58] Priya: model artifacts can be stored in your S3 with access via role. runtime only pulls artifacts from your endpoints. configs and secrets can be stored in Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault; we integrate with both.
[07:09] Dave: any gotchas for cross-account roles? we want to avoid lots of manual IAM adjustments.
[07:14] Luca: we usually request a cross-account role with narrow permissions for deployment and CR changes; for production we scale into an automation pipeline. less manual ops is better.
[07:22] Maya: ok let's recap next steps. we'll send pricing and docs; Luca will prep pilot plan and network runbook; Sara/Evan to share CIDRs, regions, and compliance checklist.
[07:31] Dave: sounds good. one more micro question - can we get flow logs from runtime traffic?
[07:35] Priya: yes you can enable VPC flow logs and we can send additional telemetry to your observability stack.
[07:41] Liam: timeline - if pilot looks good, what is typical time to production?
[07:44] Maya: usually 6-8 weeks from pilot kick-off to production for Private - depends on network approvals and procurement. Dedicated hosted can be quicker.
[07:52] Evan: procurement - will need MSA and DPA review, security addendum.
[07:56] Maya: we'll route legal templates and can start redline conversations after the pilot.
[08:00] Dave: ok thanks for the clarity.
[08:03] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and the calendar invite for the technical deep dive.
[08:08] meeting end

Notes: transcript has intermittent mis-attributions in live tool; some acronyms spoken quickly (KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash), minor filler words. references: network runbook (link: https://redwood.example.com/runbook/orion), SOC2 attestation (link: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2.pdf), pricing deck placeholder (will be sent).
